subject: orthopaedics
title: Spinal deformities: scoliosis curves and kyphosis humps

steps.tx: **Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis** affects girls far more often than boys during the growth spurt, and a right thoracic curve is commonest. The **Adams forward bend test** reveals a rib hump, while the **Cobb angle** measures curve size between end vertebrae, as this figure set shows. The Risser sign grades skeletal maturity from the iliac apophysis. Premenarchal girls face the highest risk of rapid progression.
steps.say: The figure brings together the bedside test and the measurements used for this curve. Bending forward makes the rib prominence stand out clearly on one side. Lines drawn along the end vertebrae give the angle that grades curve size. A maturity sign on the pelvis shows how much growth still remains. Girls near their fastest growth face the greatest risk of worsening.

vis.alt: A figure showing Adams forward bend test, rib hump, Cobb angle measurement on X-ray, and Risser sign for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis diagnosis.
vis.caption: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: Adams test, Cobb angle, and Risser sign. Image: Rigo M, Negrini S, Weiss HR, Grivas TB, Maruyama T, Kotwicki T, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: **Congenital scoliosis** follows hemivertebrae, unsegmented bars or fused ribs that grow unevenly from birth. **Neuromuscular scoliosis** in Duchenne disease or polio forms a long C shaped curve with pelvic tilt. A left thoracic curve or painful curve needs a spinal scan to exclude a **syrinx** inside the cord. Cardiac scanning matters when Marfan syndrome forms part of the picture.
steps.say: Some curves begin before birth because the vertebrae form or separate abnormally. Weak trunk muscles instead let the spine collapse into one long sweeping curve. Pain or an unusual left sided chest curve warns about a hidden cord problem. Imaging of the whole spine then searches for a fluid cavity inside the cord. Heart checks also matter when a tall connective tissue disorder is present.

steps.tx: Curves under twenty degrees in a mature child need observation, while a **brace** treats a growing child near **twenty to forty** degrees. The Boston brace serves most thoracic curves, and wear for many hours each day decides success. Fusion suits curves **over forty five** degrees, using posterior pedicle screw fixation in modern practice. Weaning begins near full maturity, and in brace films check the correction achieved.
steps.say: Small curves in a nearly grown child need only regular observation over time. A growing child with a moderate curve wears a brace for most of the day. Consistent brace wear will matter more than the brand name of the brace itself. Large curves that keep progressing need surgical fusion with screw fixation. Maturity signs tell the team when brace treatment can safely stop.

steps.tx: **Postural kyphosis** stays flexible and corrects when the patient stands straight, unlike a rigid structural curve. **Scheuermann disease** wedges at least three vertebrae by five degrees each and stays rigid on bending. Tuberculosis destroys the front of vertebrae and forms a sharp angular **gibbus** deformity. A growing Scheuermann curve may respond to bracing, while fixed deformity may need osteotomy.
steps.say: A flexible round back corrects when the young person makes a postural effort. Structural disease will instead wedge the front of several vertebrae and stay rigid. Spinal infection can collapse the front column and produce a sharp backward peak. Bracing helps a growing structural curve when the child wears it consistently. Fixed severe deformity may need bone cutting surgery to restore balance.

steps.tx: This lateral film shows **thoracic hyperkyphosis** with anterior wedging of consecutive vertebrae and **Schmorl nodes** at the endplates. That combination illustrates **Scheuermann disease**, which stays rigid unlike a postural round back. The image matters because wedging of at least three vertebrae separates structural disease from habit. For the exam, read the wedge angle and endplate changes together before naming the condition.
steps.say: The side film shows the chest spine curved forward more than normal. Several vertebral bodies look narrower at the front than at the back. Small disc protrusions indent the endplates and appear as labelled nodes on the film. Together those features will mark a structural growth disorder of the spine. This pattern differs from a flexible curve that corrects with posture alone.
